analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 2% excise tax on stock buybacks by publicly traded corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have taxed corporate stock buybacks at 2%, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsor beyond its two Democratic sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 2% federal tax on the value of stock that publicly traded corporations buy back from shareholders. Buybacks are how companies return cash to shareholders and push up their share price; taxing them makes that practice more expensive. The bill exempts small buybacks under $1 million, shares contributed to retirement plans, mergers, and certain dealer transactions, and it prevents the company from deducting the tax. It never advanced past its initial committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiary would have been the U.S. Treasury and general taxpayers, since the 2% tax would have raised revenue from corporations and their shareholders. Workers could have benefited indirectly if companies responded by directing cash toward wages, hiring, or investment instead of share repurchases, though the bill does not require them to do so.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 2% excise tax on the value of stock repurchased by publicly traded domestic and foreign-traded corporations, making buybacks more expensive relative to other uses of corporate cash.
Closes easy escape routes: the tax applies to economically equivalent transactions, to purchases made through corporate affiliates, and to corporations that moved overseas but kept U.S.-traded stock.
Exempts buybacks under $1 million and stock contributed to employer-sponsored retirement plans or employee stock ownership plans, so small issuers and worker pension arrangements are not hit.
Bars corporations from deducting the tax and gives the Treasury Secretary authority to write rules preventing abuse of the exemptions.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase their own stock would pay the 2% tax, and because the tax cannot be deducted, the cost would ultimately land on those companies and their shareholders — a group skewed toward wealthy households, institutional investors, and executives paid largely in stock.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations doing buybacks and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue but does not earmark it for any specific public purpose, so the benefit to ordinary people is diffuse and depends entirely on how Congress later spends it.
The bill does not require companies to redirect the money toward wages or investment; a 2% tax changes the price of buybacks but leaves the choice entirely to management.
The tax exempts repurchases that are treated as dividends under the tax code, which could let some buyback-style cash distributions escape the tax entirely.

A fair objection from the other side: many shares are held indirectly by ordinary people through pension funds and mutual funds, so reduced buybacks can slightly lower returns for everyday savers along with wealthy investors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is reasonable: a low-rate tax aimed at a concentrated practice, with carve-outs protecting retirement plans and small firms. But its real-world effect would likely be modest — 2% is small enough that most large companies doing buybacks would absorb it, and the dividend-treatment exemption leaves a visible path around the tax. It would raise real revenue and slightly reprice buybacks against investment, but it is not a transformational check on corporate cash practices.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on September 20, 2021, with Sen. Ron Wyden as the only co-sponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee that same day.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — after the referral.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations and their largest shareholders came out ahead: buybacks remained untaxed and the practice continued unchanged through the life of the bill.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 20, 2021 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no party split was ever recorded; its only recorded support was two Democratic senators, and no opponent ever acted on the record.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase stock
industries.note: A 2% excise tax on the value of shares they buy back, scaled to how much they repurchase, with the tax not deductible. Companies doing large buybacks would pay the most, and the bill would make returning cash to shareholders slightly more expensive relative to investing in the business.

industries.industry: Institutional investors, wealthy households, and executives paid in stock
industries.note: Buybacks support share prices and concentrate gains among large shareholders and stock-compensated executives; taxing them trims that channel of return. Ordinary savers with small pension or fund holdings would be touched only indirectly and slightly.
Repurchased stock contributed to employer retirement plans or employee stock ownership plans is expressly exempt from the tax, so worker pension arrangements are shielded.
